inputs.need:
I am a consultant paediatrician and the transition lead at a children's hospital. Our adolescent transition clinic sees about 400 young people a year with long-term conditions such as type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, epilepsy and cystic fibrosis as they move to adult services between 16 and 19. We use a 20-item readiness questionnaire at 14, 16 and 17 and a half, and the score is used, more than it should be, to decide when a young person is ready to transfer. Some of our young people score highly and then stop attending adult clinics within a year; others score low and we keep them in paediatrics until they are nearly 19, which they resent.

Our transition steering group is revising how we assess readiness, and I have been asked to write a narrative review that pulls together what readiness assessment tools measure, whether readiness scores predict how young people do after transfer, and what young people and families think of being assessed. The literature is scattered across conditions and professions and uses the word readiness in different ways, so I want something interpretive that helps us think, rather than a pooled number. I have two protected sessions a week for ten weeks and help from our transition nurse specialist. The review will shape a new local approach to be presented to the steering group in January 2027, and I would like it to be good enough to publish. I am particularly worried about young people with learning disabilities and those from families with low health literacy, for whom our questionnaire may not work at all.
inputs.constraints: Two protected sessions a week for ten weeks (November 2026 to January 2027) plus support from the transition nurse specialist. Published literature only; no new data from patients. Report to the transition steering group in January 2027.

records.title: Transition readiness assessment tools for adolescents with chronic conditions: a systematic review of measurement properties
records.authors: Okonkwo-Harland B, Lindstrom-Achebe T, Vasquez-Pryce M
records.venue: Journal of Adolescent Health Care Transitions
records.abstract: We identified 14 tools that assess readiness for transition from paediatric to adult care in adolescents with chronic conditions. Most were self-report checklists of disease knowledge and self-management skills, with parent versions for five. Content validity was rated adequate for eight tools and internal consistency for ten, but only three tools had been tested for whether scores predicted outcomes after transfer, and none in more than one condition. Few tools had been tested in young people with intellectual disability or in languages other than English.

records.title: Does transition readiness predict outcomes after transfer to adult care? A prospective study in young adults with type 1 diabetes
records.abstract: We followed 286 young people with type 1 diabetes who completed a readiness questionnaire at 17 and transferred to adult care by 19. Readiness scores were not associated with HbA1c or clinic attendance 12 months after transfer (odds ratio for attendance per 10-point higher score 1.04, 95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.23). Attendance was higher among those who had met a named adult clinician before transfer. The authors suggest that readiness questionnaires describe skills rather than predict engagement and should not decide the timing of transfer on their own.

records.title: Readiness as a process: young people's and parents' views of transition readiness questionnaires
records.abstract: We held conversations with 21 young people with long-term conditions and 16 parents about readiness questionnaires used in two transition clinics. Young people felt the questionnaires tested knowledge they already had and missed what worried them, such as talking to new doctors and managing without their parents. Parents wanted their own changing role to be assessed. Both described readiness as growing confidence within relationships rather than a score, and several young people said a low score had delayed their transfer against their wishes.

records.title: Structured transition programmes and attendance after transfer: a multicentre before-after evaluation
records.authors: Achterberg-Fenwick J, Olatunji-Borg S, Kristensen-Ade N
records.venue: Journal of Adolescent Health Care Transitions
records.abstract: Six children's hospitals introduced a structured transition programme with a joint paediatric and adult clinic, a named transition coordinator and readiness checklists used as conversation tools rather than thresholds. Attendance at the first adult appointment rose from 64 to 82 percent, and loss to follow-up at one year fell from 21 to 12 percent. The programme had several components, so the contribution of readiness assessment cannot be separated from the joint clinic and the coordinator. Comparison hospitals were not included.

records.title: Floor and ceiling effects of a 20-item transition readiness questionnaire across chronic conditions
records.abstract: We analysed 1,940 completed readiness questionnaires from young people aged 14 to 18 with eight chronic conditions. Scores clustered at the top of the scale from age 16 onward, with 38 percent of 17-year-olds at the ceiling, so the questionnaire could not distinguish between older adolescents. Items about medication were answered very differently across conditions, and items about adult services were often skipped. The authors recommend condition-neutral items, a wider range of difficulty and caution in using scores to time transfer.

records.title: Health literacy, deprivation and transition readiness scores in adolescents with long-term conditions
records.abstract: Among 512 adolescents with long-term conditions, lower readiness scores were associated with lower health literacy and with living in the most deprived areas, after adjustment for age and condition. Adolescents who needed an interpreter at clinic scored lowest, and the questionnaire was available only in English. The authors warn that readiness scores may partly measure literacy and social advantage, so using them as thresholds could delay transfer for disadvantaged young people. Scores were also lower when clinic letters went to a parent rather than to the young person, and the authors call for tools tested in several languages.

records.title: Assessing readiness for transition in adolescents with intellectual disability: adapting a questionnaire for proxy and supported completion
records.abstract: Standard readiness questionnaires could not be completed independently by most of 44 adolescents with intellectual disability in two transition clinics. An adapted version with pictorial items, supported completion and a carer section was completed by 40 of 44 adolescents and their carers. Carers valued questions about decision-making support and adult social care. The adapted version has not been tested for reliability or for whether it predicts outcomes, and the study was too small to compare adolescents with different levels of disability.

records.title: Timing of transfer to adult services: age-based versus readiness-based criteria
records.abstract: We compared two clinics, one transferring at a fixed age of 18 and one transferring when a readiness score passed a threshold. Readiness-based transfer happened a median of nine months later, but one-year attendance and disease control after transfer did not differ between clinics. Young people in the readiness-based clinic more often reported frustration at staying in paediatrics. The clinics also differed in staffing and joint clinics, so differences in outcome cannot be attributed to the transfer criteria alone. Fewer than a third of young people in either clinic had met an adult clinician before transfer.

## Readiness assessment: quick overview

- Readiness tools mostly measure disease knowledge and self-management skills.
- Evidence that scores predict outcomes after transfer is limited and mixed.
- Young people and parents see readiness as confidence and relationships, not a score.
- Structured programmes with joint clinics improve attendance after transfer.
- Scores may be lower in deprived and low health literacy groups.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level after a first reply arrived as markdown and was not applied. Readiness tools mostly measure knowledge and self-management skills, and few have been tested for prediction. In the one prospective study, readiness at 17 did not predict outcomes after transfer, while meeting a named adult clinician did. Young people and parents describe readiness as confidence within relationships, scores show ceiling effects and track health literacy and deprivation, and adapted versions are needed for intellectual disability. Structured programmes improve attendance, but their readiness component cannot be separated from joint clinics.

response.overview: Narrative review with a documented search and purposive selection, organised around four questions: what readiness tools measure, whether scores predict outcomes after transfer, how young people and families experience assessment, and how assessment can be fair for disadvantaged groups.
response.population: Studies of adolescents aged 12 to 19 with long-term conditions transferring from paediatric to adult care, and of their families and clinicians, published 2010 to 2026 in English.
response.exposure: Readiness assessment in any form: questionnaires, checklists, structured conversations and adapted or supported tools.
response.procedures: The lead searches three databases and two grey literature sources with a dated strategy and records it; the transition nurse specialist checks selection for a random 20 percent. Sources are chosen for relevance to the four questions, with priority to measurement studies, prospective prediction studies, qualitative studies of experience and adaptations for disadvantaged groups. Findings are synthesised thematically with the strength of evidence stated for each conclusion.

path.scan.items[1].keyFindings: Correction from the authors: after a coding error was fixed, each 10-point higher readiness score at 17 was associated with higher clinic attendance 12 months after transfer (odds ratio 1.31, 95 percent CI 1.08 to 1.59), although not with HbA1c. Meeting a named adult clinician before transfer remained associated with attendance.
